title: Language fingerprint card
description: Read by two consumers: the reader renders the prose, and tools/build compiles `tells`, `rules_out`, and `project_fingerprint` into the identifier's scoring table. The card is the single source of truth for both, so a change to a tell changes the classifier.

name.description: Display name as practitioners write it. 'C#', not 'C Sharp'.

aka.description: Alternate names and the wrong-but-common ones. Feeds search. e.g. rustlang, rs, golang, csharp, dotnet.

family.description: Drives the deck filter. `config` and `markup` matter because beginners hit YAML and JSON constantly without knowing they are not code.

likelihood.description: How probably Nyx meets this. Drives the deck's 'you will meet this' filter and breaks classifier ties toward the common answer, which is the right prior for a beginner.

extensions.description: File extensions, primary first. Leading dot required.

tells.description: The dead giveaways. Every note MUST state the tell against its nearest neighbor: not 'fn declares a function' but 'only Rust uses exactly fn; Go uses func, Kotlin uses fun, Python uses def'. That contrast is what teaches recognition, and it is also what the reader displays as evidence.

pattern.description: Literal token or regex, per `kind`. Matched against the pasted snippet.

kind.description: token matches on word boundaries. sigil and operator skip word boundaries so $, ::, and <- match. line_start anchors per line, for shebangs and directives.

weight.description: 10 is decisive on its own (`<?php`, `Cargo.toml`). 5 is strong. 2 is corroborating. Reserve 9 and 10 for tokens that appear in no other covered language.

note.description: The prose shown as evidence in the identifier. Must contrast against a neighbor language.

rules_out.description: Negative evidence. Seeing any of these means it is NOT this language, which resolves confusable pairs faster than positive evidence can.

because.description: Which language this token points at instead.

project_fingerprint.description: Often the fastest identification of all, and the only one that works on a folder rather than a snippet. Feeds both the identifier and Project Scan.

file.description: Exact filename or glob. Cargo.toml, package.json, *.csproj.

decisive.description: True when this file alone settles it. Cargo.toml is decisive; package.json is not, because it does not distinguish JS from TS.

build_dirs.description: Generated output. Large, git-ignored, safe to delete, will be rebuilt. Nyx asks this constantly.

shape.description: Structural profile. Renders as prose and feeds the classifier's punctuation scoring.

naming.description: e.g. snake_case functions, CamelCase types, SCREAMING_SNAKE constants

import_keyword.description: The word it uses. Rust says use, Python says import, C says #include. Cheap and highly discriminating.

confusable_with.description: The pairs that actually trip people: Java/C#, JS/TS, C/C++, Rust/Go, Python/Ruby. Each settle_it must be a decision she can make in two seconds by looking at the snippet.

tiebreak.description: Machine-readable form of settle_it. When both languages score within the ambiguity band, presence of `pattern` decides for `favors`.

errors_look_like.description: How to recognize this language from its failure output alone, which is often all Nyx has.

patterns.description: Regexes the identifier uses to route a pasted stack trace to this language.

meet_it_when.description: The concrete situations Nyx encounters it: an agent picks it, she clones a tool to build, she reads the source of something misbehaving.

what_agents_get_wrong.description: Required. What an agent produces in this language that looks fine and is not, and the specific thing to watch for in a diff. This is the field that makes the deck useful to a vibe coder rather than to a student.

version_landscape.description: Whether an answer found online from three years ago still applies. Python 2 vs 3 and Rust editions are opposite ends of this.

joke.description: Reserved for the 'you will not meet these' sidebar. Fortran, COBOL, Perl. At the technology's expense, never at Nyx's, and once only.
